hints: Notice the table asks about two things: separation of fringes and maximum intensity of dark fringes when only the intensity through one slit is increased.
Recall fringe separation $x = \lambda D / a$ depends on wavelength from the constant frequency, not on slit brightness, so check what changes $x$.
Think about destructive interference when the two amplitudes were equal and then unequal: can the waves still cancel to zero at a dark fringe?
walkthrough: Identify the geometry: fringe separation is $x = \lambda D / a$, where $\lambda$ is wavelength, $a$ is slit separation and $D$ is slit to screen distance.
Frequency is constant so wavelength $\lambda = c/f$ is constant, and $a$ and $D$ are not changed, so $x$ is unchanged.
Recall dark fringes need destructive interference with path difference of $(n+1/2)\lambda$ and opposite displacements cancelling.
Initially the two amplitudes are equal, so they cancel to give approximately zero intensity at dark fringes.
Increasing intensity through one slit makes its amplitude larger, so $A_1 \ne A_2$ and the resultant amplitude $A_1 - A_2$ is non-zero.
Hence the minimum intensity is now greater than zero, so dark fringes appear brighter and contrast is reduced. This is option C.

options.A: Fringe separation does not decrease because wavelength, slit separation and screen distance are unchanged, and dark fringes do change because cancellation is no longer complete.
options.B: Fringe separation does not increase because $\lambda$, $a$ and $D$ are unchanged, although the dark fringe intensity does become greater.
options.C: Separation $x = \lambda D / a$ is unchanged with constant frequency, and unequal amplitudes prevent complete destructive interference so dark fringes are brighter.
options.D: Separation is correctly unchanged, but dark fringes are no longer zero intensity because the two amplitudes no longer cancel fully.
